title: The sky as a platter
hookLine: Guru Nanak's arti: the sky is the platter, sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls

cards: Evening, in a temple. Someone lifts a metal platter of small flames and moves it in slow circles before a sacred image. There may be flowers on the plate, incense in the air, someone waving a fan.

This is arti, a ceremony of lamps in Hindu worship. Sikh tradition says that Guru Nanak, the first Sikh Guru, was at a temple during an evening arti like this, and that he lifted his eyes to the sky and sang a hymn.

teach.b: First, the platter. The hymn, found on page thirteen of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, opens with the sky itself. The sky is the platter.
In Gurmukhi: gagan mai thaal. The bowl of the heavens is the plate held up in worship. Second, the lamps.

The sun and the moon are the lamps on that platter. The circles of the stars are the pearls scattered across it. In the hymn's picture, the sky is already doing what the worshipers are doing: lifting light.
Third, the rest of the ceremony. The fragrance carried down from the sandalwood hills is the incense. The wind is the fan.

teach.h: WIND THE FAN, FORESTS THE FLOWERS.
teach.b: All the forests and their flowers are the flowers offered. Nothing has to be brought in; the whole creation is already the offering. Then the line that turns it all toward God: what an arti this is, O destroyer of fear.
The hymn goes on to say that the unstruck sound, a music no hand plays, is the temple drum.
Sikhs sing this hymn in the gurdwara, and it's part of Kirtan Sohila, the hymns recited before sleep. Notice what the hymn doesn't do. It doesn't argue.
It widens the frame, until the evening sky is holding up its own lamps to God, and anyone can stand under it.

how: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's arti hymn in the gurdwara, and it is part of Kirtan Sohila, the evening hymns recited before sleep.

o: a string of prayer beads worn in worship
a hymn sung only at sunrise to the sun
a ceremony of lamps waved before a sacred image

games.q: the sky's arti — tap the pairs.

s: in the hymn, the incense is the fragrance from the sandalwood hills
nothing has to be brought in: the creation is already the offering.
in the hymn, the drum is played by a temple drummer
the drum is the unstruck sound, a music no hand plays.
the hymn is found on page thirteen of the Guru Granth Sahib
Ang 13, and it's part of Kirtan Sohila, recited before sleep.

games.q: it's evening and a ceremony of lamps is under way. you're asked what the true platter of worship is. what do you point to?
o: the sky, with the sun and moon for lamps.
games.why: the hymn makes the sky the platter, the sun and moon the lamps and the stars the pearls.

practice: If it's evening, look out at the sky; if not, close your eyes and remember a sky you've seen at dusk.
Find the light that's left, the sun going down, the moon, a first star, and what's moving, the air, a branch, a cloud, and let it all be one slow ceremony that nobody is running.
If you pray, let the hymn's words, what an arti this is, rest in you.

wordCard.voice: Arti. The ceremony of lamps that gave Guru Nanak's hymn its shape: the sky itself as the platter, sun and moon its lamps, stars its pearls. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the sky is the platter, the opening words of Guru Nanak's arti, Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 13.

carryVoice: Your line: the sky's arti. Sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 13 (Dhanasari, Mahala 1, 'gagan mai thaal')
